MATH 014 - Introduction to Data Science¶

Project 2 (Parts 1 and 2): The IMDb Top 250 Movies¶

Group 1: Tamunoinaemi George, Andie Hilliard, Jeremiah Keeton, Ava Lewis, Kolby Mitchell, and Rebecca Tabera

Dataset Overview¶

1. Dataset Information¶

What is the title or topic of your dataset? IMDb Top 250 Movies Dataset

What is the source or link where you obtained it? https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kushwahaaa27/imdb-top-250-movies-dataset/data

Briefly describe the real-world context or purpose of this data. This data could be used to analyze which movies are the most popular and therefore make the most money. The budget information also allows studios to determine the lowest amount of money they can spend on a movie that earns a high rating online.

Introduction: This dataset analyzes the Top 250 Movies on IMDb. It breaks down the main information about each movie, such as its description, the budget, and the content rating. The dataset provides a comprehensive comparative view of the movies and all the important data about them.

Which columns are numerical? The numerical columns are (int & float): parentImdbId, startYear, endYear, budget, grossWorldwide, runtimeMinutes, averageRating, numVotes, metascore.

Which columns are categorical or object type? (verified with the built-in function select_dtypes) The categorical/object columns are: id, url, primaryTitle, originalTitle, type, description, primaryImage, thumbnails, trailer, contentRating, releaseDate, interests, countriesOfOrigin, externalLinks, spokenLanguages, filmingLocations, productionCompanies, genres, and isAdult. (Note: select_dtypes shows isAdult as a boolean column rather than an object column, since it only holds True/False.)

Do you think any data type should be converted (e.g., object → numeric or datetime)? Explain why. The metascore column is currently stored as a float, when a Metascore is traditionally a whole number, so converting it to an integer would be helpful. Besides that, none of the other column data types seem to need converting, as the data all properly correspond to the data type assigned to it.

Additional note: in the code below we also made a few optional conversions that make later analysis easier: releaseDate to datetime, contentRating to category, budget and grossWorldwide to nullable integers (they are floats only because of missing values), and the list-like text columns to real Python lists.

In [9]:
# Convert data types (work on a copy so the original stays unchanged)
df_clean = df.copy()

# Dates: text -> datetime
df_clean['releaseDate'] = pd.to_datetime(df_clean['releaseDate'])

# Low-cardinality text -> category
df_clean['contentRating'] = df_clean['contentRating'].astype('category')

# Counts / scores stored as float only because of NaN -> nullable integer
for col in ['budget', 'grossWorldwide', 'metascore']:
    df_clean[col] = df_clean[col].astype('Int64')

# List-like text such as "['Crime', 'Drama']" -> real Python lists
for col in ['genres', 'countriesOfOrigin', 'spokenLanguages', 'filmingLocations']:
    df_clean[col] = df_clean[col].apply(ast.literal_eval)

df_clean[['releaseDate', 'contentRating', 'budget', 'grossWorldwide', 'metascore',
          'genres', 'countriesOfOrigin']].dtypes

What do these statistics tell you about the numerical columns (e.g., min, max, mean, std)? The different statistics are useful for selective numerical columns. Some columns, like endYear and parentImdbId, have no data, and therefore give us no conclusions.

Other columns, like metascore and averageRating, are useful for their mean and median data. They show the average ratings of these top movies (82.77 and 8.31 respectively), which could be useful for determining the goal post to be considered a top performing movie. (Looking more closely at averageRating, the ratings only range from 8.0 for The Incredibles to 9.3 for The Shawshank Redemption, with a median of 8.2.)

The minimum and maximum startYear is useful in obtaining the oldest movie still in the top 250. The oldest top 250 movie was released in 1921.

Many columns such as startYear, budget, and grossWorldwide can be analyzed for their standard deviation values. That information could be used to investigate the impact of budgets on their overall performance and revenue. The standard deviation of grossWorldwide is about 389,728,700, showing a wide margin in overall profits. The standard deviation of budget is about 1,012,864,000, showing a wide margin in allotted budgets despite a similar performance in ratings.

The standard deviation of runtimeMinutes, which is 34.5, shows a significant deviation in the length of the top performing movies.

The mean of numVotes, which is 779,029.2, shows a high average level of audience participation towards high rated movies.

Are there any columns where the values seem unusual or inconsistent? There are two unusual columns, the endYear and parentImdbId columns. This is because they lack actual values, resulting in a count of 0 and NaN results.

Additional unusual values we found while exploring the data:

  • Budgets are in different currencies. Life Is Beautiful shows a budget of 15 billion and Spirited Away shows 2 billion, which is obviously not US dollars (compare The Dark Knight at 185 million). These budgets seem to be recorded in the local currency (lira, yen, rupees), which is why the mean budget ($134 million) is much higher than the median ($17.75 million) and the maximum is 15 billion. The budget column therefore cannot be compared across countries as it is.

  • startYear and releaseDate do not always match. 57 films have a release date whose year is different from startYear. In most cases the release date is 1-2 years later (e.g. Schindler's List: 1993 vs. 1994-02-04), probably because the release date is the first release in a particular country. The most extreme case is Kill Bill: The Whole Bloody Affair (2004 vs. 2025-12-05), which is a re-release of a recut version. So startYear is better to use when looking at when a film was made.

    print(f"{col}: {(df[col] == '[]').sum()} rows contain an empty list")

externalLinks: 62 rows contain an empty list
filmingLocations: 15 rows contain an empty list

Check for missing values in each column. Data is currently missing values in the columns endYear and parentImdbId, which are both listed as float values. When looking at the data in each column, there are also several gaps throughout the set. This can be seen in the columns metascore, budget, filmingLocations, externalLinks, contentRating, and trailer, where rows are empty or show [] with no value inside of it. (Counts: metascore is missing 20, budget 22, grossWorldwide 4, contentRating 6 and trailer 6; externalLinks has 62 empty lists and filmingLocations 15.)

Are there any duplicate rows? There are no duplicate rows found in our dataset (and no duplicate IDs or titles).

Provide your observations: The endYear and parentImdbId columns have missing data, which possibly can affect our analysis of the dataset because they contain no information at all (100% missing), so they cannot be used for any calculation and are best dropped. The gaps in metascore, budget and grossWorldwide matter more: any average, correlation or comparison using them is only based on the films that have a value, and these gaps are not random (missing Metascores are mostly silent-era and non-English films). We should not fill them with 0, since a film with a 0 budget or 0 Metascore would be wrong and would pull averages down. type and isAdult are also not missing, but they are constant (every row is movie and False), so they do not help any analysis.

Other typos / inconsistencies found:

  • There are no leading or trailing spaces in any of the text columns.
  • The contentRating labels are inconsistent. Not Rated (22) and Unrated (1) mean the same thing, so they should be merged. Approved (19) and Passed (6) are old labels from before the modern MPA system (1968), so they only appear for old films and are not comparable to R or PG, but they are real values and not errors. TV-MA (2) is a TV label that appears on two of the films.
  • Genres are listed alphabetically, not by importance. Every film's genres list is in alphabetical order, so the first genre is not the film's "main" genre (e.g. The Lord of the Rings is listed as Adventure, Drama, Fantasy simply because A comes before D before F). Because of this, we should count every genre a film has instead of only the first one.
  • primaryTitle and originalTitle are different for 53 films (e.g. Seven vs. Se7en, City of God vs. Cidade de Deus). This is not an error, since these are English vs. original-language titles.
  • Column names are in camelCase, which does not match the usual Python snake_case style, and countriesOfOrigin and spokenLanguages contain codes such as 'XWG' (West Germany) and 'SUHH' (Soviet Union) for countries that no longer exist.
In [25]:
# Clean up: drop useless columns, simplify column names, fill/standardize values
# 1. Drop columns that are empty, constant, or just web links
drop_cols = ['parentImdbId', 'endYear', 'type', 'isAdult',       # empty or constant
             'url', 'primaryImage', 'thumbnails', 'trailer',     # links
             'externalLinks', 'interests']                       # links / tag lists
df_clean = df_clean.drop(columns=drop_cols)

# 2. Rename camelCase columns to snake_case
df_clean = df_clean.rename(columns={
    'primaryTitle': 'primary_title', 'originalTitle': 'original_title',
    'contentRating': 'content_rating', 'startYear': 'start_year',
    'releaseDate': 'release_date', 'countriesOfOrigin': 'countries_of_origin',
    'spokenLanguages': 'spoken_languages', 'filmingLocations': 'filming_locations',
    'productionCompanies': 'production_companies', 'grossWorldwide': 'gross_worldwide',
    'runtimeMinutes': 'runtime_minutes', 'averageRating': 'average_rating',
    'numVotes': 'num_votes'})

# 3. Standardize content-rating labels and fill the 6 missing ones
df_clean['content_rating'] = (df_clean['content_rating'].astype('string')
                              .str.strip()
                              .replace({'Unrated': 'Not Rated'})
                              .fillna('Unknown')
                              .astype('category'))

# 4. Trim title text just in case
df_clean['primary_title'] = df_clean['primary_title'].str.strip()

Explanation for Question 6¶

This column represents the average amount of budget being spent per each minute in the overall runtime. This can be insightful for gauging the relative spending level of each movie in relation to its runtime (since longer runtimes could affect the overall budget).

Note: because many non-US films list their budget in local currency (see section 4), a few values are not real dollar amounts. For example, Life Is Beautiful works out to about 129 million per minute and Princess Mononoke to about 18 million per minute, compared to a median of about 131,000 per minute for all films.

Additional new columns¶

In [29]:
# New column 1: decade of release
df_clean['decade'] = (df_clean['start_year'] // 10) * 10

# New column 2: number of genres listed for the film
df_clean['num_genres'] = df_clean['genres'].str.len()

# New column 3: gap between critics (Metascore / 10) and IMDb users
# positive = critics liked it more than IMDb users; negative = users liked it more
df_clean['critic_audience_gap'] = (df_clean['metascore'].astype('float') / 10
                                   - df_clean['average_rating']).round(2)

# New column 4: first-listed country, and a "trustworthy" USD budget
# (budgets of many non-US films are stored in local currency, e.g. yen or rupees)
df_clean['primary_country'] = df_clean['countries_of_origin'].str[0]
df_clean['budget_usd'] = df_clean['budget'].where(df_clean['primary_country'] == 'US')

# New column 5: return on budget (only where the budget is trustworthy)
df_clean['gross_to_budget'] = (df_clean['gross_worldwide'].astype('float')
                               / df_clean['budget_usd'].astype('float')).round(2)

# New column 6: runtime category
df_clean['runtime_category'] = pd.cut(df_clean['runtime_minutes'],
                                      bins=[0, 100, 150, 1000],
                                      labels=['short (<=100 min)', 'medium (101-150 min)', 'long (>150 min)'])

What the new columns represent:

  • decade - the decade the film was made (e.g. 1990), based on start_year. This makes it easy to compare time periods.
  • num_genres - how many genres IMDb lists for the film (1 to 3).
  • critic_audience_gap - the Metascore divided by 10 minus the IMDb rating, so both are on a 0-10 scale. A positive number means critics liked the film more than IMDb users; a negative number means users liked it more than critics. It is missing when the film has no Metascore.
  • primary_country - the first country listed for the film.
  • budget_usd - the budget, but only for films whose first listed country is the US. Because many non-US budgets are in local currency (see section 4), we only keep the budgets we can trust to be in dollars. Only 142 of the 250 films have one.
  • gross_to_budget - worldwide gross divided by the USD budget, which shows how many times a film earned back its cost. The biggest earners are classic low-budget hits like Rocky (about 122 times its budget) and Jaws (about 70 times).
  • runtime_category - short (100 minutes or less), medium (101-150 minutes) or long (over 150 minutes).

Explanation for Question 7¶

We created two different subsets. The first one (imdb_df_drama) is comprised of movies that are in the "Drama" genre (179 films). This can be used to understand what percentage of high-performing movies are dramas. That understanding can be used to analyze the underperformance or overperformance of Drama movies in the Hollywood scene. The second subset (imdb_df_highbudget) is comprised of movies which have an above-average budget (30 films). This can be used to understand how higher budget movies perform in comparison to lower budget movies.

Note: the average budget is about $134 million, but it is pulled up by budgets recorded in local currency, so at least 6 of the 30 "high budget" films (Life Is Beautiful, Princess Mononoke, Spirited Away, Dangal, 3 Idiots and Your Name.) are only there because of their currency, not their real budget.

Filter 1: Films with an IMDb rating of 8.8 or higher - the "elite" group of 15 films. Almost all of them are well-known films made between 1957 and 2010, led by The Shawshank Redemption (9.3), The Godfather (9.2) and The Dark Knight (9.1). Drama, Crime and Adventure dominate. One surprise is Attack on Titan: The Last Attack (8.9), which has only about 39,000 votes compared to the millions of votes the other elite films have, so its rating is based on far fewer people.

Filter 3: Worldwide blockbusters - films that grossed at least $1 billion. 12 films reached this level, and all of them are from 1993 or later. The list is dominated by superhero and franchise films (*Avengers: Endgame* at about $2.94 billion is the highest). Their IMDb ratings are mostly high but not top-tier (8.1-8.4), except for The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (9.0) and The Dark Knight (9.1). Several also have a Metascore below 80 (e.g. Joker at 59, Infinity War at 68), which suggests critics were less impressed than audiences.

# Filter 4: films where critics and IMDb users disagree the most (gap of 1.0 point or more)
disagree = df_clean[df_clean['critic_audience_gap'].abs() >= 1].sort_values('critic_audience_gap')

print("Critics rated much HIGHER than users:", (disagree['critic_audience_gap'] >= 1).sum())

Filter 4: Films where critics and IMDb users disagree by 1 point or more (on the 0-10 scale). 100 of the 230 films with a Metascore fall in this group, split almost evenly: 51 where users liked the film much more than critics and 49 where critics liked it much more. The biggest gaps where users are more positive include Life Is Beautiful, The Intouchables and Snatch (all about -2.7 or -2.8). The biggest gaps where critics are more positive are mostly classics (Tokyo Story, Citizen Kane, Vertigo), which have a Metascore of 100 but "only" about 8.1-8.2 from users. This suggests that critics reward film history and craft, while IMDb users favor more popular, modern and emotional films.

Explanation for Question 8¶

The code above finds the categorical columns and creates a dictionary of all the unique values of those columns, each grouped based on its originating column. Categorical columns useful for analysis and grouping are the genres, spokenLanguages, countriesOfOrigin, and contentRating columns. These categories have limited unique values, allowing for grouping based upon these values.

Additional unique-value checks (on the cleaned data)¶

Important categorical variables for analysis/grouping:

  • genres - 21 different genres. Since a film can have up to 3, we count each genre separately. Drama is by far the most common (179 films), followed by Adventure (65), Crime (54) and Action (43), and Musical (2) and Film-Noir (3) are the rarest.
  • content_rating - 10 labels (after merging Unrated into Not Rated). R is the most common (103), followed by PG (37) and PG-13 (35). The old labels Approved and Passed only appear for old films.
  • decade - 11 decades from the 1920s to the 2020s. The 2000s (48 films), 2010s (44) and 1990s (39) have the most films.
  • primary_country - 23 different first-listed countries. Counting every country listed for each film, the US appears in 194 of the 250 films, followed by the UK (50), France (23) and Japan (22).
  • runtime_category - lets us compare short, medium and long films.

primary_title and description are unique for every film (250 unique values), so they are identifiers/descriptions rather than useful grouping variables.

9. Grouping and Aggregation¶

In [43]:
#9
# Group worldwide gross by genre (the group's starting code used the name "genre"; the real column is "genres",
# and each film can have several genres, so the genres are split into individual values first)
grouptest = (imdb_df.assign(genres=imdb_df["genres"].apply(ast.literal_eval))
                    .explode("genres")
                    .groupby("genres")["grossWorldwide"])
grouptest.mean().round(0).sort_values(ascending=False)

The group's starting code grouped worldwide gross by genre. It has been completed here so it runs: the genres are split into individual values first, then the average gross is calculated for each. Below we added more grouped summaries on the cleaned data.

Additional grouping¶

                       avg_votes=('num_votes', 'mean'),

What we learned (decade): The dataset is weighted toward recent decades: the 1990s-2010s together contain 131 of the 250 films, while the 1920s and 1930s only have 6 each. The average rating is quite similar across decades (between about 8.1 and 8.4), so no decade is dramatically better, although the 1990s are the highest (8.41) and the 1920s the lowest (8.13). Two things change a lot over time: the number of votes (films from the 1920s-1960s average roughly 120,000-340,000 votes, while 1990s-2010s films average roughly 0.9-1.2 million, which makes sense because IMDb users are mostly younger and watch newer films) and the Metascore (it falls from about 92-96 for films from the 1920s-1950s to about 78-81 for films since 1980, so critics rate classics very highly).

What we learned (genre): Average ratings are again very close, between about 8.1 (Sport) and 8.4 (Fantasy), so genre does not strongly decide how well a film is rated. The genres at the top of the table include some very small groups (Musical, Western and Music have only 2-6 films each), so those averages are not very reliable. Among the larger genres, Fantasy (8.41, 18 films), Crime (8.36, 54 films) and Sci-Fi (8.36, 23 films) have the highest average ratings, while Comedy (8.22) is the lowest of the large genres. Box office tells a different story: Fantasy (about $630 million), **Adventure** (about $547 million), Sci-Fi (about $528 million), **Action** (about $465 million) and Animation (about $452 million) earn far more per film than **Drama** (about $150 million), even though Drama is the biggest genre by far. So the films that make the most money are not necessarily the best rated, and Animation and Comedy films are the shortest on average (about 107-109 minutes) while History and Biography are the longest (about 146-153 minutes).

What we learned (content rating): PG-13 films have the highest average worldwide gross (about $680 million), which is more than double G (about $330 million) and PG ($268 million) and more than triple R-rated films (about $187 million), although R films are the biggest group (103). PG-13 films also have the highest average rating among the large groups (8.38) and the most votes on average. Old labels like Approved and Passed have tiny average grosses (about $5 million and $0.2 million), which makes sense because they belong to old films (the gross figures are not adjusted for inflation). The 6 films with Unknown ratings have the highest average rating (8.52), but that is a very small group.

The correlation table shows a moderate relationship between num_votes and average_rating (about 0.55) - the more people vote, the higher the rating tends to be, which makes sense since popular films attract more fans. num_votes and gross_worldwide are also related (about 0.46). The metascore has a negative correlation with start_year (about -0.42), confirming that older films get much higher critic scores. Runtime has a small positive relationship with rating (about 0.30), so longer films are slightly better rated.

Summary and Conclusion¶

10. Initial Observations¶

This dataset was interesting because it lets us look at what the best-rated movies have in common and how audiences and critics see them differently. A few patterns stood out. Ratings in this list are all very close together (8.0-9.3), so differences between decades, genres and content ratings are small; the more meaningful differences are in popularity and box office (votes, gross) and in critic scores. Critics and IMDb users often disagree: critics give the highest scores to older classics, while users rate popular modern films and crowd-pleasers higher than critics do. The list is also dominated by US films (194 of 250 list the US), by Drama (179 films), and by films from the 1990s-2010s. PG-13 films earn the most on average, and Fantasy, Adventure, Sci-Fi and Action films have the biggest box office, while Crime and Fantasy have the highest average ratings among the larger genres. Several data issues came up: two completely empty columns, constant columns, missing budgets/grosses/Metascores (often for older or non-US films), budgets stored in different currencies, hidden empty lists ('[]'), startYear that does not always match releaseDate, inconsistent content rating labels (Unrated vs. Not Rated), and lists that were stored as text. Genre lists are also alphabetical rather than ranked, so each genre had to be counted separately. The dataset is also fairly small (250 rows) and already limited to top-rated films, so these patterns say nothing about movies in general. Questions for Part 2 include: Do films with more votes really get higher ratings? Which films have the biggest gap between critics and audiences, and what do they have in common? Are US films rated differently than films from other countries? Has the average runtime of top films changed over time?

Part 2: Data Visualization¶

This part uses the same IMDb Top 250 data from Part 1. We make graphs to look at how the data is spread out, compare groups, and find relationships between columns. Every graph has a title, axis labels, an annotation (a note pointing to something important), and a short explanation.

Importing Libraries¶

In [49]:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
%matplotlib inline
%config InlineBackend.figure_format = 'retina'

Data Loading¶

The data was loaded in Part 1 (df and the cleaned copy df_clean), so we reuse it here.

Data Understanding and Cleaning Summary¶

In Part 1 we checked the data types, missing values, duplicates and outliers, and then cleaned the data: we dropped 10 empty, constant or link columns, renamed the columns, turned list-like text into real lists, changed Unrated to Not Rated, and made new columns (decade, gross_to_budget, budget_usd and others). Missing values were left empty instead of being filled with 0. Many non-US budgets are in other currencies, so budget_usd only keeps the budgets of US films (142 of 250).

For the graphs, we change money into millions of dollars so the numbers are easier to read.

What this shows: This shows how the gross (money earned worldwide) is spread out. Most movies are bunched at the low end: the frequency drops sharply as the gross gets bigger, and 83.6% of the movies earned less than $500 million. The middle (median) movie earned about $65 million, but the average (mean) is about $243 million. The mean is higher because a few huge hits pull it up. Only 12 movies earned over $1 billion. The biggest outlier is Avengers: Endgame at about $2.9 billion.

What this shows: This shows how many times, on average, movies earned back their budget in each decade. This helps us find "golden ages" and "dark ages" of movie profits. The 1970s were the golden age (about 37 times the budget on average), mostly because of huge hits like Rocky (about 122 times) and Jaws. After the 1970s the ratio dropped and stayed between about 5 and 11. The 1930s also look high, but that is mostly one outlier, Gone with the Wind (about 101 times). The 1920s look very low (about 0.09). Only movies with both a US budget and a gross are counted, so the early decades have very few movies and their averages are less reliable.

Section II: Relationship Visualizations¶

3.1 Scatter plot: budget vs. IMDb rating¶

In [54]:
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))
plt.scatter(df_clean["budget_millions"], df_clean["average_rating"], s=25, alpha=1, color="orange")
plt.title("Budget vs. IMDb Rating (US films)")
plt.xlabel("Budget ($ millions)")
plt.ylabel("IMDb average rating")
plt.annotate("12 Angry Men: rated 9.0\nwith a $350 thousand budget", xy=(0.35, 9.0), xytext=(40, 9.1),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
plt.annotate("Avengers: Endgame:\nbiggest budget, only 8.4", xy=(356, 8.4), xytext=(220, 8.7),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
plt.show()

print("Correlation between budget and rating:", round(df_clean["budget_millions"].corr(df_clean["average_rating"]), 2))

Correlation between budget and rating: 0.05

What this shows: There appears to be little to no correlation between rating and budget, since the dots do not move in a certain direction as the budget goes up. The correlation is about 0.05, which is almost zero. Cheap movies and expensive movies are both rated about 8 to 9. The outliers are 12 Angry Men (rated 9.0 on a budget of only $350 thousand) and *Avengers: Endgame* (the biggest budget at $356 million, but only rated 8.4). This means that spending more money does not make a movie rated higher, which answers the question in our introduction about the lowest amount a studio can spend on a highly rated movie.

3.2 Pair plot of the main numeric columns¶

In [55]:
four_cols = df_clean[["average_rating", "num_votes", "gross_millions", "runtime_minutes"]].astype("float")
sns.pairplot(four_cols)
plt.suptitle("Pair Plot: Rating, Votes, Gross and Runtime", y=1.02)
plt.show()

What this shows: The pair plot compares every pair of columns. The graphs on the diagonal show how each column is spread out (for example, most movies have a low gross). Where the dots tilt upward, the two columns are related. Votes and rating tilt upward, so movies with more votes tend to be rated higher. Votes and gross also tilt upward, so popular movies earn more. Runtime and rating show a weaker upward trend. The outliers are the dots far away from the rest: the billion-dollar movies in the gross column and The Best of Youth, which is the longest movie at 374 minutes. We used only four columns so that each graph is easy to read.

3.3 Heatmap of correlations¶

In [56]:
corr = df_clean[["average_rating", "num_votes", "metascore", "runtime_minutes", "gross_worldwide", "start_year"]].astype("float").corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap of the Numeric Columns")
plt.xlabel("Red = both go up together, blue = one goes up while the other goes down")
plt.show()

What this shows: A number close to 1 means two columns go up together, and a number close to -1 means one goes up while the other goes down. The strongest relationship is votes and rating (0.55), and votes and gross (0.46) is also fairly strong. Metascore and release year (-0.42) is negative, so newer movies get lower critic scores. Metascore and rating (0.07) is almost zero, so critics and IMDb users do not rate movies the same way. There are no very strong correlations, and correlation does not prove that one column causes the other.

Summary and Conclusion (Part 2)¶

Our graphs show these main patterns:

  1. Most movies earn a modest amount, and a few earn a lot. The median gross is about $65 million, but outliers like *Avengers: Endgame* (about $2.9 billion) pull the average up to about $243 million.
  2. PG-13 movies have the biggest budgets (about $132 million on average), more than double G, PG and R movies.
  3. Movies earned back the most compared to their budget in the 1970s, because of hits like Rocky and Jaws. The ratio has been lower since.
  4. A bigger budget does not mean a higher rating (correlation about 0.05). 12 Angry Men is a very highly rated movie with a tiny budget, while Avengers: Endgame has the biggest budget and only an 8.4 rating.
  5. Popular movies tend to be rated higher. Votes are related to rating (0.55) and to gross (0.46).
  6. Critics and IMDb users do not rate movies the same way. Metascore is almost unrelated to rating (0.07), and critics give lower scores to newer movies (-0.42).

Limits: The data only has 250 movies that were already rated very high, so these results do not describe all movies. Some budgets are in other currencies, so we only used US budgets (142 films), some values are missing, and the gross numbers are not adjusted for inflation.

What this means for our question: A studio does not need a huge budget to make a highly rated movie, but a bigger budget and a PG-13 rating are linked to a bigger box office.
